rows.text: Recovery after process failure, suspend/resume and loss of network access.
rows.evidence: Two of three clauses are test-covered; see asserted_by. CORRECTED 2026-09-10: this field previously named docs/benchmarks/namespace-memory-attribution.json, a heap-attribution artifact with no bearing on recovery -- a copy artifact from generating the ledger. CORRECTED AGAIN 2026-09-11: it then said the suspend/resume clause is unmeasured, which had stopped being true. It was measured (docs/benchmarks/service-lifecycle-and-suspend.json): the daemon came back from a suspend as the same process, same MainPID and ActiveEnterTimestamp, mount and index intact. That run's own verdict is why the row is still open, and it is a better reason than 'unmeasured': the cycle was two seconds of s2idle, too short to expire a token, tear down a network or lapse a subscription. A real access token lives about an hour and a measured subscription held 2,999,973 ms. So the shallow end of the clause holds and the end that matters is untested. Registered for the run that would close it: docs/benchmarks/deep-suspend-beyond-token-lifetime.json -- deep S3 rather than s2idle (this machine supports it; mem_sleep reads '[s2idle] deep', so the earlier run was shallow by setting and not by hardware, which that artifact had inferred wrongly), 90 minutes via rtcwake, and delivery of a change made after the wake. scripts/suspend-check.py captures the before state and compares it after, because a process on the machine being suspended cannot observe its own suspend. UPDATE 2026-09-13: process failure and network loss are now seen on a real desktop, not only in tests: an Ubuntu 24.04.4 VM with a signed-in OneDrive (docs/benchmarks/vm-recovery-and-real-desktop.json). SIGKILL of the daemon -> systemd restart, ready in 13s. The cable pulled for three minutes -> both feeds offline, the mount listing locally throughout, ready again 116s after the cable returned, the journal naming the stop and the return. A power cut (QMP quit) with a save one second old -> the journal opened and remounted ready in ~80s. One finding worth its own fix: the save caught in flight ended 'failed' (its payload not yet durable) and is not counted by stuck_changes, so it shows only in Recent activity, not in the attention count or tray -- P5 in that artifact. rows.text: Real token expiry/refresh and visible reauthentication when consent expires.
rows.evidence: Partial: the installed daemon refreshed its Microsoft grant hourly for 1.5 days without intervention (journal, 2026-09-07..09), which evidences real token refresh. The visible half is now covered end to end by tests rather than at its last hop only. CORRECTED 2026-09-11: this field said consent expiry 'cannot be scheduled'. Waiting for a grant to lapse on Microsoft's timetable cannot; REVOKING it can, and from the daemon's side that is the same event -- the token stops working and no refresh will fix it. Registered in docs/benchmarks/revoked-grant-and-reauthentication.json, with the clauses that matter beyond the state itself: that it is visible without reading a log, that the mount and the offline copies survive a credential problem, and that reauth restores the account without resetting the index or dropping pins. RUN 2026-09-13 (docs/benchmarks/revoked-grant-and-reauthentication.json), and the row is still not ticked. What was measured, against a real account: a refused grant is noticed without intervention and made visible without a log -- the tray reached NeedsAttention with the tooltip 'work-onedrive: sign-in required' -- and the mount, the cached listing and the pinned file all survived it, the pinned file reading in full to its checksum while access was refused. Recovery was automatic: re-enabling sign-in was enough, refresh succeeded at 09:29:39 and both feeds were ready by 09:30:40, with indexed_items, the pin and the cached listing unchanged against a reference taken before the withdrawal. WHY IT IS STILL OPEN: two things the run deliberately did not reach. The grant was WITHDRAWN by disabling the enterprise application's sign-in rather than by revoking consent, because the app has no verified publisher and re-consent could have needed an administrator; that tests the same daemon-side event and less of the consent cycle. And because recovery was automatic, `cirrove reauth` restoring an account was never exercised -- the better outcome for a user and the weaker one for this clause. A SEPARATE CONCERN FOUND BY THE RUN: the daemon wrote no journal entry at all when authorization was refused. The state reaches a user through the tray and `cirrove status`, which is what this row asks, but an operator reading the journal sees a healthy daemon and nothing says what the provider refused or why.
rows.asserted_by: The refresh half: cirrove-auth tests simultaneous_expiry_rotates_once_and_stale_401_cannot_expire_new_token, credentials_are_not_used_when_rotation_cannot_be_persisted, and explicitly_granted_write_scope_survives_refresh_and_keyring_roundtrip. The visible half is now whole: read_only::an_expired_grant_is_shown_as_needing_sign_in_and_not_as_being_offline drives a provider that refuses the grant and asserts the feed reaches sign_in_required -- with an unreachable provider first as the control, so a daemon that called everything sign_in_required would fail it; manager::tests::a_feed_needing_sign_in_is_not_hidden_by_one_that_is_merely_offline holds the ordering into the account state a caller reads, and fails if a noisier feed is allowed to win; and cirrove-desktop/tests/accounts.rs renders that state. The median reproduces closely. The tail is worse, not better -- maximum 1184.9 ms against 834.5, and 8 to 12 samples over 500 ms rather than 6. rows.text: Reclaim inactive namespace views with correct FUSE lifetimes; pass the 500,000-file traversal, invalidation and 24-hour churn memory gates in [namespace memory](adr/0005-namespace-memory.md). Content-cache limits do not satisfy this requirement.
rows.evidence: CORRECTED 2026-09-11: this field named only docs/benchmarks/namespace-memory-attribution.json, the 2026-09-08 attribution run, and so still described a gate that has since closed. G3 -- released PSS minus indexed baseline, at most 256 MiB -- failed at 476.4 / 514.8 / 546.7 MiB and now reads 13.3 / 16.1 / 16.3 (docs/benchmarks/namespace-trim-closes-g3.json, 2026-09-10). The reclamation tick returns the pages once a mount has shed its views and gone quiet, which was the plausible outcome all along: 96.4-96.8 percent of the retained RSS was allocator-held free arena and not live data. It is a hard assertion in the fixture now, not a reported number. WHAT REMAINS, and it is not addressed by trimming at all: the traversal PEAK. traversed_with_old_files holds 492.8 / 490.7 / 504.1 MiB at 750,438 live views, and returning pages afterwards cannot lower a high-water mark reached while the views were held. Only shedding does. The number that work turns on is 637-657 bytes per live view, which reproduces to within 0.2 percent while retained RSS varies by 6 percent -- so a peak budget is a budget on concurrent live views, and at 650 bytes each a 256 MiB peak buys about 413,000 against the 750,438 held here. Two further gates in ADR 0005 are also unmet and neither is a measurement: G2 needs an evictable-bytes counter that does not exist, and G7's plateau tolerance must be fixed from a two-hour pilot before its twenty-four-hour run. THE PEAK HAS NO LIVE DESIGN, and that is the honest state rather than a gap in effort: two have been written and both were killed by their own gating measurement. Shedding -- emit notify_inval_entry above a ceiling -- needed about 1,400 per second to bind during a traversal and sustains about 107 under concurrent lookups (inval-entry-rate.json, 2026-09-08). Its successor ADR 0006, shortening the entry TTL above a ceiling so the kernel's own dentry reclamation does the work, is marked 'rejected by its own measurement' (2026-09-09): the peak does not move. ADR 0005 carried both the retirement and, in a later paragraph, the claim that the measurement had never been taken; corrected 2026-09-12. What is left is named there and neither half is small: reduce bytes per view, which three passes have moved 15-20 percent each and which will not reach a factor of two alone, or decline to resolve views beyond a ceiling at all -- a change to the lookup contract rather than to reclamation, which needs its own ADR and does not have one.

rows.text: Crash/fault tests at every durable transition and concurrent remote edits.
rows.evidence: docs/benchmarks/durable-transition-crash-coverage.json and durable-transition-sites.json for process death: all 31 runtime durable transitions are crossed by a process that then dies, measured rather than read. 2026-09-11, faults below the process: docs/benchmarks/journal-under-io-faults.json. A dm-flakey device switched to error_writes at runtime and back. What was durable before the fault survives it and reads back byte for byte afterwards; new work is refused as JournalError::Storage rather than as corruption -- reporting a refusing device as a corrupt journal would send a user to recovery steps that destroy work the device still holds. A prediction failed usefully: the journal cannot be OPENED on a failing device, because opening opens SQLite and SQLite writes. So its contents are inaccessible during a fault, which is not the same as lost, and the run makes only the second claim. A LYING FSYNC ran the same day: dm-flakey drop_writes acknowledges the write and discards it, and the journal detected it -- sealing was refused as JournalError::Stale, because the journal reads back what it wrote and finds the generation unchanged. Work durable before the lie reads back byte for byte afterwards. The claim is that this injection did not produce wrong-and-confident data, not that no discard can. TORN WRITES were attempted and are inconclusive: corrupt_bio_byte flips a byte in EVERY write bio, so it corrupts ext4's metadata as readily as the journal's data, and the phase hung. A hang in that state is a statement about ext4 meeting corrupted metadata, not about the journal. The targeted version of the same question is already answered -- overwriting a sealed payload makes recovery fail. THE POWER CUT WAS RUN on 2026-09-13 and holds (docs/benchmarks/journal-under-power-cut.json): 585 generations acknowledged durable, the machine's power removed mid-write, and afterwards the journal opened, produced generation 585 byte for byte, and sealed new work again. Verified as a real power loss rather than a reboot: the previous boot's journal ends mid-kernel-message with no shutdown sequence. PREVIOUSLY RECORDED AS STILL OPEN: The fixture for it now exists and is registered in docs/benchmarks/journal-under-power-cut.json -- seed writes ~68 acknowledged generations a second and never stops, so a cut cannot land on an idle journal, and recover asserts that everything acknowledged before the cut reads back byte for byte and that the journal takes new work again. It was exercised against process death first, which proves the mechanics and nothing about durability, and it was shown to FAIL when the acknowledged payload is altered or removed. What is left is a person and a power cut; that is the whole of what this box still needs, and it is why it is not ticked.

See docs/benchmarks/durable-transition-sites.json. a_journal_on_a_failing_device_refuses_without_losing_what_was_durable runs in three phases against one dm-flakey device in CI; re-run with the sealed payload deliberately overwritten, its recover phase fails. Its lie and after_lie phases run in CI on the same device; the tear phases exist but are deliberately not wired in, for the reason recorded in the artifact. a_journal_survives_the_machine_losing_power_mid_write is the power-cut fixture: proven to discriminate against altered and missing acknowledged payloads, and deliberately not wired into CI, because CI cannot cut power and a green run there would assert nothing. The concurrent-remote-edits clause is held by mutations::worker_exposes_content_conflict_after_a_lost_rename_instead_of_acknowledging_a_new_base, which is the combination rather than either half: the rename's response is lost -- the fault -- and the remote content changed underneath while it was, and the worker must expose a conflict instead of acknowledging a new base. lost_success_reconciles_after_restart_without_a_second_mutation covers restart-plus-reconciliation, and uncertain_deletion_needs_review_and_does_not_loop_or_block_other_files covers an uncertain outcome that must not retry blindly. The daemon answers a new `paths` verb -- up to 200 mount-relative paths per request, each with kind, pin cover (direct / inherited from a recursive folder pin / none) and bytes on disk -- so a file manager asks once per listing. packaging/nautilus/cirrove.py (nautilus-python) draws a badge on pinned items (check when the content is on disk, synchronising while fetching, none on the on-demand majority), adds a Cirrove column with the words, and offers Keep offline / Stop keeping offline on selections and folder backgrounds, recursive for folders; after an action it invalidates the item so Files asks again. Every call is off the UI thread with a 3 s timeout; no daemon or an older one draws nothing. Seen in a real Files window on this machine against the live daemon (Nautilus 50, nautilus-python 4.1): a check on a recursively pinned folder in both grid and list view, none on its on-demand neighbours, the pinned file at the mount root likewise; Files asks one entry at a time and the answers arrive within the same second for a seven-entry folder. Two wrong turns on the way, both recorded in docs/desktop.md#files: Python threads stand still inside Files, and the completion must name the provider Files passed in. NOT DONE: a refresh when a pin changes behind Files (the extension re-asks when Files re-lists or after its own actions, not on a daemon event), and the menu action exercised by hand. UPDATE 2026-09-13: the extension also implements Nautilus.PropertiesModelProvider, so Alt+Enter on a file shows a Cirrove section -- availability, bytes on this computer, whether a pin keeps it, cloud location, provider item id. The standard properties (size, MIME type, modified time, permissions) were verified correct on the live mount. UPDATE 2026-09-13 (badges): the badges are Cirrove's own icons rather than the desktop's generic ones -- a blue cloud with a check for kept and present, a cloud with a down arrow while content arrives (down because that is the direction; the tray's up arrow means a save on its way out), both with a white rim because Files draws them over a thumbnail of any colour. On this machine the generic emblem-ok-symbolic and emblem-synchronizing-symbolic resolved to a thin grey tick and circular arrow that said nothing about a cloud and did not match the tray. The generic names are still used where the branded icons are not installed, because Files draws nothing at all for a name no theme provides -- a missing badge, not a plain one. Checked against the live account: the extension resolves the branded names, a pinned file carries the kept badge and an on-demand neighbour none.
rows.asserted_by: engine::pinning::path_states_tell_a_direct_pin_from_an_inherited_one_and_from_none and ::what_is_on_disk_is_counted_from_the_block_files for the daemon's answers; scripts/test-nautilus-extension.py for the extension: mount lookup (longest mount wins), badge and column words per state, menu wording, batching at the daemon's ceiling against a fake socket, and no-daemon / refusing-daemon drawing nothing. scripts/test-nautilus-extension.py Properties tests hold the section's key/value pairs for kept, on-demand, partial, folder and refused states. The Emblems tests hold the choice between icon sets both ways, and assert that every name the extension can use is a file the tree ships -- a name without a file is a badge that silently vanishes. The badge-mapping tests now pass the name set in rather than reading the module's, which had made them pass or fail by whether the machine running them happened to have Cirrove's icons installed.

rows.text: Actionable errors, progress, cancellation and conflict resolution.
rows.evidence: PARTIAL 2026-09-11. Conflict resolution has its first real piece, and it was built because the daemon could strand a change in silence: fourteen folder removals ended in Conflict on a live drive, hiding the directories in the mount while leaving them in the account, with no status field saying so and no way to clear them -- request_mutation_retry refuses Conflict by design and nothing else touched one. AccountStatus.stuck_changes now reports them and `cirrove discard-stuck` abandons them. Measured end to end on that drive: 14 abandoned, 14 back in view, 10 deleted cleanly on the second attempt, 4 conflicted again on stale ETags and cleared after the delta feed caught up. Final state: no leftovers, nothing stuck. NOT DONE: removals only -- a stuck creation or move leaves the local tree depending on it and is refused rather than half-handled; discard only, never retry; no per-item view, so a user sees a count and not which paths; neither the window nor the tray shows it; and progress and cancellation are untouched. FIXED 2026-09-13: the count is no longer a number nobody reads. It travels on the event channel (Event::Account gained stuck_changes, serde(default) so an older daemon reads back as zero and an older client ignores the field), and the tray raises the icon to NeedsAttention, names it in the tooltip -- 'ready, 3 changes not applied', the healthy state beside it because that is what makes it surprising -- and offers 'Discard N changes the cloud refused' in the menu, shown only when there is something to discard. The menu entry calls discard-stuck over the control socket, which is allowed because it is a shortcut to a CLI command and not the only way there; leaving a user informed and helpless was the worse failure. NOT DONE still: no per-item view, so a user sees a count and not which paths, and the window shows nothing. UPDATE 2026-09-13: the count of refused changes and the Discard action are in the window as well as the tray: a 'Changes the cloud refused' row with the count, shown only while there is something to discard, and a Discard button that asks the daemon and reports what it could unwind. Progress and cancellation of transfers remain NOT DONE.
rows.asserted_by: mutations::only_changes_the_daemon_has_stopped_retrying_are_counted_as_stuck and ::discarding_refuses_anything_it_cannot_unwind_cleanly at the journal level, plus writable_session::real_a_delete_the_provider_refused_can_be_abandoned_and_the_folder_returns through a real kernel FUSE mount, which fails without the restore by never bringing the folder back. Nothing asserts the freshness caveat -- the fixture's mount does not re-observe provider changes without an explicit refresh -- so that is recorded in docs/validation.md as a live measurement instead of claimed as covered. desktop::window every_account_action_is_offered_from_the_window_and_only_where_it_applies clicks Discard and requires the discard-stuck request at the fake daemon and the row gone once the daemon reports none remain.

rows.text: Show recent activity -- remote changes from the delta feed and local saves from the upload journal, with each entry's state -- in the window, and a short form of it in the tray menu. "Recent" means changes to content, not files the user merely opened: a mount stages cache on every read, so a touched-files list would be noise. This is a log and not a level, so it does not ride the coalescing event channel, which by design hands a lagging client current state instead of the entries it missed; it needs its own query. File names appear in the menu and in the window, never in the tray tooltip, which is shown on hover without intent and is visible to anyone looking at the screen or a shared one; the tooltip carries a count. Provide a setting to turn the listing off entirely.
rows.evidence: PARTIAL 2026-09-13. The daemon records what the delta feed delivers from the second delta on -- the first lists the whole drive and a re-baseline does the same, and neither is activity -- in a bounded in-memory ring per account, with names (a deletion's name read from the index before the page publishes), and answers `recent` with those and the journal's latest saves, states included, item ids resolved to names through the index. The window shows a Recent activity group when there is anything, cloud changes first, the refused saves marked; the tray shows five lines under each account's entry, fetched after each account event; `cirrove recent` prints both. Seen live: a fresh daemon lists its journal's recent uploads. NOT DONE: the ring forgets on restart (by design, but the window then shows only the journal side until the feed moves); no times shown for local saves (the journal has none); nothing distinguishes added from changed, because the feed does not.
rows.asserted_by: service::recent::tests::the_ring_keeps_the_latest_and_lists_them_latest_first; engine::discovery::recent_changes_are_recorded_from_the_second_delta_on_and_not_on_a_reset (baseline records nothing, a continuation records the delivered folder with its name, a reset records nothing); desktop::window every_account_action_is_offered_from_the_window_and_only_where_it_applies renders the cloud change and the refused save from a fake daemon's `recent` answer; tray::menu::tests::recent_lines_appear_under_their_own_entry_only_when_there_are_any_and_do_nothing.
